player: I swing my cudgel at the hound before it reaches me.

turns.input: I swing my cudgel at the hound before it reaches me.
turns.passage:
Your hand closes on nothing. The cudgel is not at your belt, and the swing you meant to throw goes out into rain and empty air. You have no weapon at all.

The hound is still a stride away, claws skidding on the slick stones as it drives toward you. Its breath steams in the cold, and its eyes stay fixed on your throat. It is coming, and there is no time to find anything else to hold.

Your bare fists are all you have, and the hound is almost on you.

player: I try to talk the eel seller down to half price for the whole barrel.

turns.input: I try to talk the eel seller down to half price for the whole barrel.
turns.passage: The seller's mouth tightens, and for a moment she looks past you toward the other stalls as if hoping someone will rescue her from you. Then she sighs and slaps a wet palm on the barrel's rim. "Half. For the whole barrel. Don't think I'll forget how you did that." She wipes her hands on her apron, still eyeing the purse at your belt. "Pay now, or the eels go back to the water, and I'll be dickering with the next buyer for the same price you just talked out of me."

player: I study the rider on the ridge: who are they, what do they carry?

turns.input: I study the rider on the ridge: who are they, what do they carry?
turns.passage: You shade your eyes against the last of the dusk and fix on the far ridge. The grey horse stands like carved stone against the sky, and the rider has not moved once. You shift your weight off the road's rut and tilt your head, trying to pick out the cut of their cloak, the shape of whatever is strapped behind the saddle, and any sign of colour or device that would tell you whose they are.

turns.input: success_at_cost:cost.exposure
turns.passage:
The last of the dusk drains away while you hold your eyes on the ridge, and the details come clear. The rider wears a long grey coat cut for riding, its hem stiff with mud. Lashed behind the saddle is a bundle of oilcloth wrapped tight around something square and heavy, a box or a case, with its corners bound in tarred cord. There is no crest and no colour, nothing that says whose errand this is.

Then the head turns. Not quickly. The rider looks down the slope, straight along your line of sight, and holds it there. Nell Upton lifts one gloved hand from the reins and lets it fall again. It is not a wave.

The grey horse stays exactly where it is, but you have the feeling you have been seen properly now, and that whatever you do next, the rider will be watching for it.

turns.input: I creep along the wall's shadow and slip past the sentry to the postern.
turns.passage: You fit yourself into the deepest part of the wall's shadow, every step placed on the stone's uneven edge where it cannot ring. Above you the sentry turns at the end of his beat, lantern swinging out over the parapet, then swinging back. The postern door waits in darkness beyond him, a few strides past where his path bends. Your breath slows. Watch the lantern.

turns.passage:
Your foot finds a loose stone at the bend, and it rocks with a dry scrape. The lantern stops mid-swing. Quill Kettle turns, and the light finds the edge of your cloak before you can pull it back into the dark. He does not shout. He rests a hand on the parapet and studies the place where you stand, the way a man counts coins he suspects are short.

The postern is still a few strides past his beat, its door black and unguarded. He is between you and it, though, and he is no longer looking at the lantern. He is looking at you.

player: I grab the drunk by the collar and pin him against the wall.

turns.input: I grab the drunk by the collar and pin him against the wall.
turns.passage: Your fist closes on his collar and his own momentum does the rest. He hits the tavern wall with a dull thud, and the lantern beside the door swings and steadies. He is heavier than he looks, but he is too drunk to fight you properly. His arms flail, then go slack against the stones. The sour reek of spirits rolls off him. Behind him the tavern door hangs open, spilling warm light, the clatter of mugs, and a fiddle that has lost its tune. The drunk squints at you, eyes swimming, and blinks like he is only now noticing who has him. Whatever he does next, you have him here, and you can choose how long you keep him.

player: I put my shoulder to the hatch and heave it open.

turns.input: I put my shoulder to the hatch and heave it open.
turns.passage:
You stand at the foot of the cellar stair, the air thick with damp and the smell of old wet wood. The hatch above you is swollen into its frame, and the beam pinning it looks rotten along its underside, grey and soft where your thumb presses it. Somewhere beyond the boards, water drips at a steady pace.

Your feet find a footing on the lowest step. You can feel how the wood will give or refuse before you ever push, and you set your weight back, ready to lean in with everything you have.

turns.passage:
You brace your shoulder under the beam and drive upward until the rotten wood cracks along its length. It sags, then drops a shower of grey pulp across your hair and collar. The hatch lifts with a groan and swings back on its hinges, letting in a breath of cold air from the room above.

It takes longer than you hoped. Your arms are shaking, and the steady drip beyond the boards has not stopped, so you have spent more of the night here than you meant to. Grit crunches under your boots as you shift your weight.

Above the open hatch, a dim strip of lamplight shows along the edge of a floorboard. Someone's footsteps pass overhead and then stop.

Behind him the alley narrows toward a rain-slick stair, and his guard is wide open on the side where you cut him. He is still dangerous, and he is breathing hard. Your move.

player: I roll clear, grab my axe from the dirt, and swing at him again.

turns.input: I roll clear, grab my axe from the dirt, and swing at him again.
turns.passage: You roll hard to the side, out from under Marek's raised blade, your shoulder grinding into the packed dirt. Your fingers close on the haft of your axe as you come up, and his boot comes down where your head was a heartbeat ago. He is breathing hard, his eyes flicking from your hands to the weapon. Whether you get clear of his reach before he commits again depends on how quick you are right now.

turns.input: commit
turns.passage: You roll wide and come up fast, the axe haft still in your fist, and for one clean moment you have your feet under you and a yard of space between you and Marek. Then he doesn't give you the rest of it. His blade comes around low and fast, quicker than the look in his eyes warned you it would be, and it bites into your side as you rise. The pain folds you half over. Your breath comes in ragged pulls, and there is blood warm under your coat. Marek stands square in the lamplight, shoulders heaving, his mouth set in something close to a grin. He is not hurrying now. He is waiting to see whether you can still lift that axe.

player: I shout for the watch at the top of my lungs.

turns.input: I shout for the watch at the top of my lungs.
turns.passage: Your shout tears through the Alley and bounces off the brick walls. Somewhere up the lane a shutter bangs open and a voice calls back, but no boots are running yet. Marek Voss's blade has already found you. The cut burns along your side, and you are worn, your breath short and your footing less sure than it was. Marek doesn't lower his steel. His eyes flick past your shoulder toward the sound, then return to you. He shifts his weight onto the balls of his feet, the way a man does when he has decided not to wait for help. The lane is narrow, and the mouth you came in by is behind him.

player: I break away and run down the alley.

turns.input: I break away and run down the alley.
turns.passage: You plant a shoulder into Marek's chest and twist, trying to tear your collar from his fist. His grip is iron, and the stone is cold against your back. Beyond his elbow, the side alley opens into darkness, a few strides away, with a stacked crate blocking part of its mouth. Marek's breath is hot and sour as he leans in, already shifting his weight to bar your way. Every instinct says move now, before he sets his feet.

He is not far, a few strides at most, and he is already coming after you with a low, furious grunt. The alley runs on ahead, narrowing toward a rain-slick gap and a faint glow beyond it. Your footing is good, but he is close enough to grab you again if you slow.

The price of that blow lands on you too: a hot, dragging ache that makes you grit your teeth. Sill answers with a wild hook that whistles past your ear and smacks the wall behind you. He circles left, favouring his weight, watching you the way a man watches something he has just learned to respect. Behind him Marek lies still in the dirt, breathing slow and ragged. Sill has not found his footing yet. You can press the gap while he is off balance, or take a breath and look for a way to keep him from reaching you again.

player: I ask Ola Brandt what she knows about a man called Tam Harlan.

turns.input: I ask Ola Brandt what she knows about a man called Tam Harlan.
turns.passage: Ola doesn't turn from the water right away. When she does, her eyes go over you once, slowly, the way she'd check a fare before taking their coin. "Tam Harlan. Yes, I know the name." She sets the pole against the rail. "He's crossed on my boat more than once, and he's never paid me what he owed. That's all I'll say about him from this landing." She nods toward the lights across the water. "If you're going after him, he's most often at The Night Dock. Go by the back steps, and keep your hands where people can see them."

player: I ask Mother Aldis what happened to the roof.

turns.input: I ask Mother Aldis what happened to the roof.
turns.passage: Mother Aldis doesn't look up at the broken roof right away. When she does, her eyes stay on the timbers hanging over the nave, not on you. "The wind took the north slates in the storm, and the rest came down after it. That's what I told the parish, and it's what I'd like to believe." She turns her folded hands over. "But the bell-door was barred from inside when I locked up at vespers. This morning it stood open to the weather, and I have not yet found anyone willing to say why." She studies your face, weighing whether you are a threat to her or a help. "You're not from the diocese, and you're not from the Night Dock. So tell me plainly what you want with my chapel."

player: I ask Corvin what the east gate is like.

turns.input: I ask Corvin what the east gate is like.
turns.passage: Corvin turns his cup slowly in his hands before he answers. "East gate? Busy by day, a sour mess after the bell. Two guards on the arch, and the sergeant there, a big man with a cough, will look at your papers for longer than he needs to, especially if you're carrying anything heavier than a purse." He glances toward the door and lowers his voice. "The gate shuts at the second bell. Anyone still outside after that pays the watch to be let in, and they don't write down what they paid." He takes a sip. "Why do you ask? You don't look like a man with papers to hide, but you look like someone who's thinking about getting through it."

player: I ask Brother Hale what he wants.

turns.input: I ask Brother Hale what he wants.
turns.passage: Brother Hale turns from the vault door at last, and the lantern light shows a face drawn tight with something close to fear. His hands are knotted together in front of his robe. "I want you to step back," he says, his voice low, as if the stone itself might be listening. "Whatever you came here to take, it is not yours to take. And the price of it will fall on people who never asked for it." He glances past your shoulder toward the stair, then back to you. He is waiting to see whether you will listen.

player: I ask the carter who might know where the butcher went.

turns.input: I ask the carter who might know where the butcher went.
turns.passage:
The carter takes the straw from his mouth and looks past you toward the yard, where the lamps are going out one by one. "Butcher's been gone since the bell rang twice. Didn't say where. He doesn't talk much, and he talks less when he's scared." He spits into the dust. "If anyone's heard which way he went, it's Tam Harlan. He drinks at The Night Dock and listens to everyone who does. Sela Vey's down there too. She knows which doors in this town open for coin and which ones open for a knife."

He goes back to chewing, then adds, quieter, "Tell Tam I sent you. He won't like it, but he'll talk."

The road down to the river is dark, and the Night Dock's lanterns are the only light in it.

player: I look around the yard.

turns.input: I look around the yard.
turns.passage: The yard is cobbled and damp, lit by a lantern hung on a post near the stable doors. Hay and wet leather hang in the air. Carts stand against the far wall, one with its shafts propped up on a block, and a rain barrel near the kitchen door has a film of ash floating on it. The kitchen door is shut now, a thin line of light showing beneath it. Joss is leaning on a pitchfork by the stalls, watching you without much interest. The gate to the street is barred from this side, and the wall beside it is low enough to climb if you had reason to. Beyond the wall, the sound of the river carries up from the Night Dock.

player: I ask Dowl whether the gate was locked last night.

turns.input: I ask Dowl whether the gate was locked last night.
turns.passage:
You kneel beside Dowl and say the question aloud, low, as if he might still hear it. Nothing answers. His eyes stay open on the rafters, and the cold lantern at his side gives no sign of whether it was lit when he died. The silence is its own kind of answer: he never got the chance to tell anyone what he saw at the gate.

The gatehouse is small. The great bar and the iron ring of the main gate are a few steps away, past the narrow window where the night air leaks in. Someone may have left marks on the bar, or dropped something near the lock. Whoever was last to touch that gate was not Dowl, or he would not be lying here.

Your choice is where to look first: the body, the lantern, or the gate itself.

player: I hand Imre the sealed letter and ask her to carry it north.

turns.input: I hand Imre the sealed letter and ask her to carry it north.
turns.passage: Imre takes the letter and weighs it in her palm without opening it. Her thumb rubs the seal once, the way someone checks a coin. "North, then. Three days if the Ferry Road bridge holds, four if it doesn't, and I'm not carrying anything past the toll gate without knowing its weight." She tucks the letter inside her coat. "I'll take it. My price is forty silver before I leave the yard, and whatever the road adds to the risk after that. And I want to know what it is you're sending. Stolen goods, a debt, a warrant? Tell me that, and we'll see whether the price stays where it is."

player: I ask the twins whether they saw who left the cart.

turns.input: I ask the twins whether they saw who left the cart.
turns.passage: The taller twin keeps a hand on the cart's broken axle and doesn't look up right away. "We were under the wheel, not watching the road," they say. The other twin glances toward the dark bend past the cart, then back at you. "Somebody had a lantern, maybe. Or maybe it was the moon on the mud. We didn't stop to ask." Their voices are flat and careful, the way people speak when they've already decided how much they'll give. "If you want names, the Night Dock is where people sell what they've pulled off roads like this. Don't say you heard it from us."

player: I watch the heron.

turns.input: I watch the heron.
turns.passage:
You crouch at the edge of the reeds and watch the marsh heron. It does not move. Its grey neck is folded into its shoulders, and its yellow eye stays fixed on the black water in front of it. Mist lies low across the shallows, and the night sounds of frogs and insects rise and fall around you.

Then the heron moves. One long leg lifts, hangs in the air, and sets down again without a ripple. It is patient in a way you recognise from your own hours of waiting. Something small shifts beneath the surface, and the bird's head tilts a fraction, just enough to show it has noticed.

Across the water, the lights of The Night Dock glow faintly through the fog. Tam and Sela are waiting there.
